title: LCIA Challenge Decision — Decision 13 (01/08/2019)
text:
DECISION RENDERED ON 1 AUGUST 2019
Subject: The Respondents challenged the entire Tribunal (entirely selected by the LCIA
Court) pursuant to Article 10.3 of the LCIA Rules 2014.
Outcome: Rejected
Seat: London, England
Governing Law of English law
the Contract:
Summary: The challenge related to certain procedural decisions made by the Tribunal.
The Respondents argued that the Tribunal imposed “new pre-conditions” to
the permission to supplement and amend their defence and counterclaims
which the Respondents claimed had already been granted to them following
instruction of new counsel.
The Respondents also contended that the Tribunal's decision to stay the
arbitration pending determination of the challenge provided an additional
ground for challenge, because the stay entailed deferral of the Tribunal's
consideration of the Respondents' request that the Claimant's claim be
treated as withdrawn in accordance with Article 24.6 of the LCIA Rules (by
reason of the Claimant's alleged failure to make timely payment of deposits
directed by the LCIA).
The Respondents further averred that they “ha[d] justifiable doubts as to the
independence of the members of the Tribunal moneywise” in light of the
“insistence on the payment of deposits, timely linked to the date at which
procedural decisions were to be rendered, at a stage in the proceedings where
there was nothing else to be done than wait and see the brief”, which made
them “fear that actions of the Tribunal might be dictated by something else
than justice”.
The LCIA Court rejected the challenge.
As London was the seat of the arbitration, the law applicable to the challenge
was English law – considered together with the relevant provisions of the LCIA
Rules.
Articles 14.4 and 14.5 of the LCIA Rules give the Tribunal the widest discretion
in relation to procedural decisions. This discretion, combined with the
applicable criteria to determine challenges based on an alleged lack of
impartiality or independence under English law, stand as obstacles to a

challenge being mounted on the basis of disagreement or dissatisfaction with
procedural decisions of the Tribunal.
The LCIA Court did not accept the Respondents' key submission that the
Tribunal, having granted them an unconditional permission to amend their
defence and counterclaims, subsequently imposed new pre-conditions to that
permission. The Tribunal had never granted the Respondents an unconditional
permission to amend their defence and counterclaims.
The Tribunal cannot be faulted for not “explicitly directing the Respondents”,
in its initial order, “to provide reasons justifying the proposed amendments, in
addition to the extent of those amendments”. It was implicit in the initial order
that the Respondents would need to set out the reasons justifying their
request in order to be granted permission to supplement or amend their
counterclaims.
Amendments and the addition or modification of claims can be disruptive to
the procedural timetable of an arbitration, and a party could disrupt the
procedural timetable applicable to the arbitration simply by notifying a
replacement of its legal representatives.
The Tribunal’s decision to stay the proceedings pending determination of the
challenge does not raise a justifiable doubt as to the Tribunal’s impartiality in
the circumstances.
The decisions to make calls for deposits belong to the LCIA Court, and these
are made in an administrative capacity. Nothing suggests that any influence
was exerted in this case in order to seek to manipulate the financial decisions
of the LCIA Court to the detriment of the Respondents or, to cite the
Respondents’ words, that the actions of the Tribunal “might be dictated by
something else than justice.”
Decision 13 - 2

Decision 13 - 4

I. OVERVIEW
1. This decision determines, in the name of the LCIA Court, an Application by the First and Second
Respondents under Article 10 of the LCIA Arbitration Rules effective 1 October 2014 (the Rules)
challenging the independence and impartiality of the three members of the Tribunal selected and
appointed by the LCIA Court (collectively, the Tribunal) to resolve a dispute between the Parties (the
Challenge).
2. After careful consideration of the facts, the law applicable to the Challenge and the Parties’
submissions, I conclude that none of the grounds raised in support of the Challenge gives rise to
justifiable doubts as to the Tribunal’s impartiality or independence, or establishes a failure on the part
of the Tribunal to act fairly or impartially as between the Parties.
3. The Challenge is therefore dismissed. The costs of the Challenge, including the Legal Costs incurred in
connection therewith, are deferred, to be determined and apportioned by the Tribunal as part of its
decision under Article 28 of the Rules.
II. FACTUAL BACKGROUND
The Parties
4. The Claimant in the arbitration is […] a company incorporated in Italy which [deals with shipping
infrastructure]. The Claimant is represented by [A].
5. The First Respondent in the arbitration is […] a company incorporated in Switzerland which is the
principal company of the [Company Group B], a reputed high-end luxury [product] group. The Second
Respondent in the arbitration is […] a company incorporated in the Isle of Man that holds certain
intellectual property rights of the [Company Group B]. The First and Second Respondents were
previously represented in the arbitration by [C]. The Respondents are now represented by [D].
Decision 13 - 5

6. The Claimant and the First and Second Respondents are collectively referred to herein as the Parties.
The Underlying Dispute
7. The underlying dispute is described briefly, merely to provide context, as the Challenge is unrelated
to the substance of the underlying dispute.
8. On or about 19 September 2014, the Claimant and the Respondents entered into a[n] […] Agreement
(the “Agreement”). A stated purpose of the Agreement was for the Parties “to collaborate in creating
a strategic design, licence and marketing alliance, combining their luxurious brands into exceptional
product offering in each of their respective fields for the best of their interest.”
9. The Agreement contains an arbitration clause providing for the settlement of disputes by arbitration
under the Rules. It also contains a clause providing that it shall be “governed by and construed,
performed and enforced in all respects in accordance with the laws of the United Kingdom”.
10. The Claimant commenced arbitration by a Request for Arbitration dated 25 April 2016, which was filed
with the LCIA on the following day. The Claimant stated that it incurred significant costs as part of the
joint promotional activities contemplated in the Agreement, and that it did not receive payment for
these services. The Respondents denied the claim and alleged that, in any event, the amount claimed
was inflated.
11. On 7 June 2016, the LCIA informed the Parties that, in accordance with Article 16.2 of the Rules and
in default of an alternative agreement between the Parties, the seat of the arbitration would be
London, England.
12. The Tribunal was appointed by the LCIA Court on 8 June 2016. An agreed procedural timetable was
established early in August 2016, and the case thereafter progressed through the written phase of the
arbitration, with the Parties’ filing of their respective statements of case, defence and response.
Decision 13 - 6

13. Between April and August 2018, the arbitral proceedings were suspended while the Parties engaged
in settlement discussions. The settlement discussions ultimately failed and the proceedings resumed
in September 2018.
Procedural History of the Challenge
14. On or about 5 September 2018, new counsel were instructed to represent the Respondents in the
arbitration. On that same date, Respondents’ newly-instructed counsel requested to be authorized to
submit a supplementary brief “to clarify the extent to which Respondents’ defence and counterclaims
as submitted by previous counsel are maintained, amended and augmented following change of
counsel”. (Respondents’ Challenge dated 12 November 2018, para. 18)
15. On 12 September 2018, the LCIA directed the Claimant and the Respondents to pay a deposit of
£ 40,000 each to the LCIA for the future conduct of the proceedings. On the same date, the Claimant
commented on the Respondents’ request of 5 September 2018.
16. On 26 September 2018, the Tribunal granted the Respondents permission to submit, by 24 October
2018, “a short application, not exceeding 15 pages, submitting as to which extent they seek to
maintain, augment and/or amend their counterclaims” (the 26 September Decision).
17. On 24 October 2018, the Respondents wrote to the Tribunal to request a temporary stay of the arbitral
proceedings or a one-month extension of the deadline for submitting the application contemplated in
the 26 September Decision. In support of the request, the Respondents explained that
the First Respondent had “very recently” filed a “criminal complaint in relation to, inter alia, the
conclusion, termination and exploitation of the Agreement”, and that they were therefore unable
to file their submission by the deadline set by the Tribunal in its 26 September Decision.
Decision 13 - 7

18. Following subsequent exchanges of communications between the Parties and the Tribunal, by
decision dated 29 October 2018, the Tribunal dismissed the Respondents’ request for a one-month
extension of time or a temporary suspension of the proceedings, and directed that the Respondents
file their application for amendment by 2 November 2018 (the 29 October Decision). The relevant
paragraphs of the 29 October Decision read as follows:
Having reviewed the submissions by both sides, the Tribunal finds that Respondents have not made
out a case to justify their requests for either a one-month extension for filing an application for
permission to amend their counterclaims or for a temporary suspension of the proceedings.
The Tribunal, through its communication dated 26 September 2018, had granted Respondents
permission to submit a short application stating to which extent they seek to maintain, augment
and/or amend their counterclaims. In such application, Respondents would be required to justify the
basis behind and extent of their amendment request, i.e., Respondents would be required to show
that certain new facts have come to light which Respondents could not have reasonably known about
earlier or new developments have taken place, which might necessitate an amendment of their
counterclaims.
The Tribunal is not persuaded that the institution of criminal proceedings by Respondents prevents
them from filing such application.
Further, the Tribunal finds that Respondents have not provided any reasons to justify the basis for
seeking a one-month extension of time or a temporary suspension of the proceedings.
Accordingly, the Tribunal dismisses Respondents’ requests as stated in their correspondence of
24 October 2018 as maintained in subsequent correspondence.
Consequently, Respondents are directed to file their application for amendment of their
counterclaims, if any, by Friday, 2 November 2018.
Furthermore, the Tribunal understands that an additional reminder of a call for further payments of
advances has been communicated by the LCIA to the Parties.
19. On 1 November 2018, the Respondents informed the Tribunal and the LCIA Court that: “[t]he
independence and impartiality of the three members of Tribunal is today, and shall be challenged in
more detail within 14 days from the last communication from the Tribunal”. Later that day, the
Tribunal acknowledged receipt of the Respondents’ correspondence and reminded the Parties that
the arbitration was continuing and that they were still required to comply with the procedural
Decision 13 - 8

timetable. Still on 1 November 2018, the Respondents reiterated that the Tribunal was challenged
“today”, that they could not comply with the 29 October Decision, and that they would not participate
in the arbitral proceedings pending determination the Challenge. The Respondents also asserted that
the Tribunal’s email of that day constituted further evidence of its lack of impartiality.
20. On 5 November 2018, the LCIA wrote to the Parties indicating that, by reason of insufficient deposits,
the Tribunal had been advised to refrain from doing further work and the LCIA Court would not be
able to determine the Challenge.
21. On 12 November 2018, the Respondents filed a submission setting out the grounds in support of their
Challenge of 1 November 2018, and confirmed their request for the revocation of the Tribunal
pursuant to Article 10.1 of the Rules.
22. On or about 13 November 2018, the LCIA reiterated that the LCIA Court would not be able to
determine the Challenge until the Parties have filed their share of the requested deposit to cover the
work required to determine the Challenge. In the event, the Respondents and the Claimant’s shares
of the deposit were respectively received by the LCIA on 3 May 2019 and 13 May 2019. The Challenge
was thereafter referred to the LCIA Court.
23. On 16 May 2019, the Presiding Arbitrator, on behalf of the Tribunal, informed the Parties and the LCIA
Court that the Tribunal had no comments on the Challenge. The Tribunal noted further that it had
decided to stay the arbitral proceedings pending a decision on the Challenge by the LCIA Court. On
the same day, the Respondents reacted to the Tribunal’s decision to stay the proceedings by
requesting the opportunity to supplement their Challenge with this new fact. According to the
Respondents, the Tribunal’s decision to stay the arbitration provided an additional ground for the
Challenge because it entailed a deferral of the Respondents’ request, on 14 and 15 May 2019, that the
Decision 13 - 9

Tribunal consider the Claimant’s claims as withdrawn pursuant to Article 24.6 of the Rules (see below,
paras. 39 and 76-85).
24. On 24 May 2019, the Claimant and the Respondents both filed submissions in relation to the
Challenge. These submissions are summarised later in this decision.
25. On 13 June 2019, the LCIA Court appointed the undersigned, [. . .], to determine the Challenge. The
Parties were notified of this appointment on the same day.
26. By letter dated 24 June 2019, I informed the parties of the procedure I was proposing to follow to
determine the Challenge. I also described to the Parties the documentation relating to the Challenge
that had been provided to me by the LCIA.
27. Considering that the Parties had already filed extensive submissions on the Challenge, I proposed to
establish a short briefing schedule that would afford the Parties and the Tribunal an opportunity,
should they wish to do so, to complete the submissions already made, and to add to the
documentation in my possession whatever additional documents they considered relevant to the
Challenge. The proposed schedule was the following :
– The Respondents may file short, final supplemental submissions, and additional documents deemed
relevant to the Challenge, by Tuesday, 2 July 2019;
– The Claimant may file additional comments on the Challenge, as well as additional documents deemed
relevant, by Monday, 8 July 2019; and
– The Tribunal may provide comments on the Challenge by Wednesday, 10 July 2019.
I indicated to the Parties that I would thereafter take the matter under advisement and seek to
determine and communicate my decision on the Challenge as soon as possible.
Decision 13 - 10

28. On 28 June 2019, the Presiding Arbitrator notified the Parties, the LCIA Court and the undersigned,
that the Tribunal had no comments on the Challenge.
29. Also on 28 June 2019, the Respondents wrote to accept the procedure proposed in my letter of 24
June 2019. The Respondents also advised that they had no additional fact or additional comment to
make in support of the Challenge, all the while reserving their right to respond “to any determination
of the Tribunal and of the Claimant”.
30. On 2 July 2019, the Claimant confirmed that the procedure proposed in my letter of 24 June 2019 was
acceptable to it and undertook to file any further submissions of the Claimant by 8 July 2019, in
accordance with the proposed timetable.
31. On 8 July 2019, the Claimant confirmed that it would make no further submission in connection with
the Challenge, relying instead on the submissions which it had made on 24 May 2019.
32. By email dated 9 July 2019, having received confirmation that neither the Tribunal nor the Parties had
any additional comments to make in respect of the Challenge, I informed the Parties that I considered
the Challenge proceedings closed and would therefore turn to determine the Challenge.
III. SUMMARY OF SUBMISSIONS
33. The following main submissions have been filed in connection with the Challenge:
a) the Respondents’ “Challenge to the Tribunal’s impartiality and independence (Art. 10.1 and 14.4 (i) of
the Rules)” dated 12 November 2018 (the 12 November Submission);
b) the Claimant’s Response to the Challenge, dated 24 May 2019 (the Claimant’s Submission); and
c) the Respondents’ Supplementary Brief, also dated 24 May 2019 (the Supplementary Brief).
Decision 13 - 11

34. The Parties’ main submissions in respect of the Challenge are summarised below to provide context.
The present decision is based on the full submissions made by the Parties in connection with the
Challenge, all of which I have carefully considered.
Grounds for the Challenge
35. The Respondents state that the Tribunal “deliberately violated” its duty pursuant to Article 14.4 (i) of
the Rules to “act fairly and impartially as between all parties, giving each a reasonable opportunity of
putting its case and dealing with that of its opponent(s)” (12 November Submission, para. 4.3).
36. The Respondents predominantly take issue with the 29 October Decision, by which the Tribunal
denied their request for a temporary suspension of proceedings or a one-month extension of time,
having found that the Respondents had not provided sufficient reasons to justify the request. The
Respondents state that while the 26 September Decision granted a permission “within limits but
unconditionally” (para. 4.3.1(a)), “the Tribunal added pre-conditions to Respondents’ submission that
were not in the 26.09.2018 permission” (para. 4.2). In that regard, they refer to the mention in the
29 October Decision to the effect that the Respondents would need to “justify the basis behind and
extent of their amendment request, i.e., Respondents would be required to show that certain new
facts have come to light which Respondents could not have reasonably known about earlier or new
developments have taken place, which might necessitate an amendment of their counterclaims”
(para. 4.2, citing the 29 October Decision).
37. The Respondents take the position that the “new preconditions” added in the 29 October Decision
“do not make any reasonable sense” and that the 29 October Decision “not only contradicts
the 26.09.2018 permission but negates it”. They also state that it was impossible for them to comply
with these pre-conditions within four days (para. 4.3.1).
Decision 13 - 12

38. The Respondents contend that the ex-ante limitations provided for in the 29 October Decision prove
that “the Tribunal has acted in deliberate violation of the Respondents’ right.” According to the
Respondents, a “party appointing new counsel at still such an early stage of the proceedings is to be
given the unconditional right to amend and supplement defence and counterclaims submitted by
previous counsel if nothing in the procedural rules forbids it”. In any event, they submit that the fact
that a criminal complaint had been recently filed by one of the Respondents should be sufficient to
justify the requested stay or extension (para. 4.3.2). According to the Respondents, the
29 October Decision “is evidence of a real possibility that the Tribunal is biased” (para. 4.4.1).
39. As noted already, the Respondents also contend that the Tribunal’s decision of 16 May 2019 to stay
the arbitration pending determination of the Challenge provided an additional ground for the
Challenge. This is because the stay entailed deferral of the Tribunal’s consideration of the
Respondents’ request that the Tribunal consider the Claimant’s claim withdrawn in accordance with
Article 24.6 of the Rules, by reason of the Claimant’s alleged failure to make timely payment of its
share of the deposit that had been called by the LCIA (Respondents’ email dated 16 May 2019 to the
LCIA).
40. Finally, the Respondents aver that they “have justifiable doubts as to the independence of the
members of the Tribunal moneywise” in light of the “insistence on the payment of deposits, timely
linked to the date at which procedural decisions were to be rendered, at a stage in the proceedings
where there was nothing else to be done than wait and see the brief”. The Respondents conclude by
stating that this insistence makes them “fear that actions of the Tribunal might be dictated by
something else than justice” (para. 4.4.3).
The Claimant’s Response to the Challenge
Decision 13 - 13

41. In response to the Challenge, the Claimant submits that there is “nothing to suggest a want of
impartiality or independence” of the Tribunal and that there is “no suggestion of any type of bias –
actual or apparent” (para. 1.4). Even if there is no allegation to that effect, the Claimant notes that
“[n]one of the three Tribunal members has any relationship with the Claimant”, and recalls that each
of them was selected and appointed by the LCIA (Claimant’s Submission, para. 2.1 and 2.2).
42. With respect to the main ground advanced by the Respondents in support of the Challenge, the
Claimant states that, in the 29 October Decision, the Tribunal simply asked the Respondents to
provide, within four working days, an explanation as to why amendments to the defence and
counterclaim should be made. In the Claimant’s view, it should have been relatively easy for the
Respondents to explain the reasons for the proposed amendment in the form called for by the
Tribunal if, by 5 September 2018, they had identified the points which they would wish to advance by
way of an amendment. The Claimant argues that the 29 October Decision was not a new order, but
rather “simply an explanation of what (self-evidently) should have been the content of the submission
in relation to the application for leave” (paras. 3.5 to 3.9).
43. Turning to the Respondents’ suggestion that the Tribunal’s decisions were influenced by monetary
issues, the Claimant states that the calls for deposits were made by the LCIA in an administrative
capacity, in accordance with the Rules, and do not imply any want of independence on the part of the
Tribunal (paras. 3.10 to 3.11).
44. The Claimant also maintains that the Tribunal’s decision of 16 May 2019 to stay the arbitral
proceedings pending a decision on the Challenge is a reasonable course of action in light of the
position and attitude adopted by the Respondents (paras. 3.12 to 3.13).
Decision 13 - 14

45. All in all, the Claimant avers that the Tribunal has always acted fairly and impartially as between the
Parties.
46. The Claimant insists that it should not be financially prejudiced by the Challenge. Accordingly, the
Claimant is seeking – from the LCIA Court or the Tribunal – costs in relation to the Challenge on an
indemnity basis and without having in any way to account for the LCIA Court’s or the Tribunal’s costs
and expenses occasioned by the Challenge.
The Respondents’ Supplementary Brief
47. In their Supplementary Brief, the Respondents list and comment on the correspondence exchanged
between the Parties and the Tribunal since the filing of their 12 November Submission.
48. The Respondents take issue with the fact that the Tribunal did not dismiss the Claimant’s claim in spite
of the fact that the Claimant’s share of the deposit was received by the LCIA Court on 13 May 2019,
that is, after the 10 May 2019 deadline. In this respect, the Respondents argue that the “Tribunal has
no issue restricting Respondents’ rights, and imposing Respondents sanctions without warning (The
Tribunal’s 29.10.2018 decision imposing new preconditions for the brief to fulfil within 4 days) but is
incapable of doing what it said it will do when it comes to sanction Claimant” (Supplementary Brief,
p. 12).
IV. APPLICABLE LAW AND CRITERIA TO BE APPLIED
49. The Parties having opted for LCIA arbitration, and London being the seat of the arbitration, the law
applicable to the Challenge is English law, to be considered together with the relevant provisions of
the Rules.
50. Under Section 33(1)(a) of the Arbitration Act 1996 (the Act), an arbitrator must “act fairly and
impartially as between the parties”. As a corollary, Section 24 of the Act provides that a party may
Decision 13 - 15

seek the removal of an arbitrator if “circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to his
impartiality”.
51. Article 10.1 of the Rules, for its part, provides that any arbitrator’s appointment may be revoked
where “circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to that arbitrator’s impartiality or
independence” (emphasis added).
52. The requirements of impartiality and independence are to be applied from the point of view of a fair-
minded and informed observer. Lord Hope of Craighead, concurring in Porter v. Magill,1 laid out the
test for reasonable apprehension of bias under English law as being “whether the fair-minded and
informed observer, having considered the facts, would conclude that there was a real possibility that
the tribunal was biased”. This test was applied by LCIA Divisions acting under the Rules2. It was also
applied to decide challenge applications under the UNCITRAL Rules in arbitral proceedings seated in
London3.
53. In a recent decision, the English Commercial Court summarised as follows the main authorities relating
to Section 24 of the Act, including as regards the notion of the “fair-minded and informed observer”:
(1) The common law test for apparent bias is reflected in section 24 – see, for example, Laker Airways
v FLS Aerospace [1999] 2 Lloyds Rep 45, per Rix J at [48]; A v B [2011] 2 Lloyds Rep 591 per Flaux J at
[21]-[29]; Sierra Fishing Co & Others v Farran & Others [2015] EWHC 140 (Comm), [2015] Lloyds Law
Reports per Popplewell J at [51];
(2) The common law test under section 24 is whether “the fair minded and informed observer, having
considered the facts, would conclude that there was a real possibility that the tribunal was biased” –
1 2002 2 AC 357.
2 See, for instance, LCIA Reference No. 142683, Second Challenge, paras. 168-170 (16 December 2016); LCIA
Reference No. 163283, para. 104 (3 October 2016); LCIA Reference No. 142683, First Challenge, para. 293 (4
August 2016); LCIA Reference No. 152906 (25 May 2016), para. 29; LCIA Reference No. 142862, para. 52 (2 June
2015); LCIA Reference Nos. 81209 and 81210, paras. 3.1 and 3.2 (16 November 2009) 27 Arbitration
International 455); LCIA Reference No. 81160, para. 3.4 (28 August 2009) 27 Arbitration International 442; LCIA
Reference No. 81224, para. 3.5 (15 March 2010) 27 Arbitration International 461.
3 See, for instance, LCIA Reference No. UN163459, para. 56 (23 October 2017); LCIA Reference No, UN152998,
para. 36 (22 June 2015).
Decision 13 - 16

see Porter v Magill [2002] AC 357 per Lord Hope at [103]; Helow v Secretary of State for the Home
Department [2008] UKHL 62, [2008] 1 WLR 2416, per Lord Hope at [1]-[3];
(3) Such a fair minded and informed observer, although not a lawyer, is assumed to be in possession
of all the facts which bear on the question and expected to be aware of the way in which the legal
profession operates in practice – see Rustal v Gill & Dufus [2001] 1 Lloyd's Law Reports 14; Taylor v
Lawrence [2002] EWCA Civ 90, [2003] QB 528; A v B [2011] 2 Lloyds Rep 591 per Flaux J at [21]-[29];
(4) A “fair-minded” observer reserves judgment until he/she has seen and fully understood both sides
of the argument: his/her approach must not be confused with that of the person who has brought the
complaint, the assumptions made by the complainer are not to be attributed to the observer unless
they can be justified objectively: A v B at [26] and Helow at [1]-[3];
(5) An “informed” observer takes a balanced approached and appreciates that context forms an
important part of the material to be considered: A v Bat [26] and Helow per Lord Hope at [3].4
54. The foregoing principles have been applied by the undersigned in deciding the Challenge.
V. ANALYSIS
Admissibility
55. The Challenge is based on Articles 10.1(iii) and 10.2(ii) of the Rules. Under Article 10.3 of the Rules, a
party intending to challenge an arbitrator must deliver a written statement of the reasons for its
challenge “within 14 days of becoming aware of any grounds described in Articles 10.1 or 10.2.”
56. There is no dispute as to the timeliness of the Challenge. The main target of the Challenge is the
Tribunal’s 29 October Decision, which was communicated to the Parties by email of even date. On
1 November 2018, the Respondents informed the Tribunal and the LCIA that the independence and
impartiality of the Tribunal was being challenged. On 12 November 2018, the Respondents amplified
the grounds for the Challenge in their 12 November Submission. I therefore find that the Challenge
was timely filed and is admissible.
4 Cofely Limited v. Bingham & Knowles Limited [2016] EWHC 240 (Comm), at para. 72.
Decision 13 - 17

Merits
57. The three main grounds raised by the Respondents in support of their Challenge are addressed in turn,
namely those related to (1) the 29 October Decision, (2) the calls for deposits to cover arbitration fees,
and (3) the Tribunal’s reaction to the late receipt of the Claimant’s deposit by the LCIA. The
Respondents’ complaint about the Tribunal’s email of 1 November 2018 is discussed last (4).
1. The 29 October Decision
58. The Respondents’ decision to bring the Challenge was triggered by the 29 October Decision. The
relevant part of the 29 October Decision has already been cited. The Respondents say that this
decision imposed “new pre-conditions” to the permission to supplement and amend their
counterclaims that had been given to them by the Tribunal on 26 September 2018.
59. In my opinion, the Respondents misconstrue the Tribunal’s 26 September Decision. The Respondents
aver, in their 12 November Submission (at para. 4.3.1(e)) :
Respondents were permitted to supplement and amend their counterclaims following change of
counsel as is expressly stated in the Tribunal’s 26 September Decision.
Such a permission obviously implies that Respondents were – given change of counsel, reason why
permission was asked – at liberty to amend and supplement their brief as they would seem adequate
and relevant, especially at a stage where everything was not said in the briefs and pre-hearing written
submissions were still due by both parties.
60. As I read the Tribunal’s 26 September Decision, the Tribunal did not grant Respondents permission to
supplement and amend their counterclaims. Rather, what the Tribunal did was to direct the
Respondents to file an application explaining the amendments they were seeking to make to their
counterclaims. This appears from the language used by the Tribunal in the relevant paragraphs of the
26 September Decision, which read as follows:
Decision 13 - 18

“1. Respondents are at liberty to submit a short application, not exceeding 15 pages, submitting as to
which extent they seek to maintain, augment and or amend their counterclaims, Respondents may
file this application within 28 days, thus by Wednesday, 24 October 2018.
2. Claimant may submit a response, not exceeding 15 pages, to the Respondents’ application within
28 days thereafter, by Wednesday, 21 November 2018.
3. Subsequently, the Tribunal shall decide on Respondents’ application seeking an amendment, if any,
of their counterclaims.”
[Emphasis added, emphasis in the original omitted]
61. As can be seen, paragraph 1 of this decision directed the Respondents to submit, by way of a short
application, “as to which extent” they were seeking to amend their counterclaims. Paragraph 3
explicitly provided that the Tribunal, after receiving the Claimant’s response to the application, would
afterwards decide “on the Respondents’ application seeking an amendment”. The language used by
the Tribunal lends no support to the Respondents’ interpretation of the 26 September Decision as
granting them permission “to supplement and amend their counterclaims”.
62. The context in which the 26 September Decision was made only serves to confirm its limited scope. In
response to the Respondents’ application to file a supplementary brief (see Respondents’ email of
5 September 2018, quoted at para. 18 of the 12 November Submission), the Claimant had observed
that it was difficult to comment on the Respondents’ request to amend, since “[o]ther than a change
of Counsel, no real explanation is given as to why the Respondent feels it needs to submit a
Supplementary Brief” (Claimant’s email of 12 September 2018, quoted at para. 21 of the 12 November
Submission).
63. In view of the language used by the Tribunal and the context of its decision, it is abundantly clear that
the application due on 24 October 2018 pursuant to the 26 September Decision was not the amended
counterclaims per se, but rather the application to obtain permission to supplement or amend the
counterclaims.
Decision 13 - 19

64. Having found that the 26 September Decision merely directed the Respondents to submit an
application seeking permission to amend their counterclaims, I cannot accept the Respondents’ key
submission that the Tribunal, having granted them an unconditional permission to amend on
26 September 2018, imposed new pre-conditions to that permission in its 29 October Decision, thus
negating the permission
65. I do not consider that the Tribunal can be faulted for not explicitly directing the Respondents, in its 26
September Decision, to provide reasons justifying the proposed amendments, in addition to the
extent of those amendments. In my opinion, it was implicit in the 26 September Decision that the
Respondents would need to set out the reasons justifying their request in order to be granted
permission to supplement or amend their counterclaims.
66. Article 22.1(i) of the Rules provides that a party wishing to supplement, modify or amend any claim
should seek the permission of the Tribunal to do so. Although Article 22.1 of the Rules makes no
mention of it, it would be expected of a party presenting an application to modify or amend a claim
to provide reasons in support of the application, irrespective of the occurrence of a change in the
party’s legal representatives.
67. As regards the change in the Respondents’ legal representatives, I should mention, even though it is
not strictly necessary to support my conclusion on the Challenge, that I do not accept the
Respondents’ submission that a party appointing new counsel should be given an unconditional right
to amend and supplement the defence and counterclaim submitted by previous counsel if nothing in
the procedural rules forbids it (see 12 November Submission, para. 4.3.2(e)).
68. Amendments and the addition or modification of claims can be disruptive to the procedural timetable
of an arbitration, as the other party has the right to be afforded the opportunity to respond to the
Decision 13 - 20

amendment, or defend against the new claims. The “unconditional right” invoked by the Respondents
would have far reaching consequences if a party could disrupt the procedural timetable applicable to
the arbitration simply by notifying a replacement of its legal representatives.
69. I also disagree with the Respondents’ assertion that the four-day delay provided for in the 29 October
Decision was unreasonable, and I reject any notion that it evidences bias on the part of the Tribunal.
In light of the fact that the Tribunal had previously granted 28 days to the Respondents (and their new
counsel) to file their application, coupled with the fact that the Respondents waited until the
expiration of this delay to seek a temporary stay of the arbitration or an extension of time, the delay
appears quite reasonable. It must also be recalled that the Respondents had first requested
permission to amend their defence and counterclaims on 5 September 2018, that is, almost two
months before the deadline of 2 November 2018 set by the Tribunal in its 29 October Decision for the
submission of the Respondents’ application for permission to supplement or amend their
counterclaims.
70. All in all, I am of the view that the Tribunal did not violate its duty, under Article 14.4(i) of the Rules,
to give the Respondents a reasonable opportunity of putting their case. In my opinion, a fair minded
and informed observer, having considered the facts, would not see a real possibility that the Tribunal
was biased when making its 29 October Decision. Rather, all indications are that the Claimant is
correct in submitting, in its correspondence dated 15 May 2019, that this ground for the Challenge “is,
in effect, no more than an appeal against a procedural order which [the Respondents] did not like.”
71. Articles 14.4 and 14.5 of the Rules give the Tribunal the widest discretion in relation to procedural
decisions. This discretion, combined with the criteria summarised above to determine challenges
based on an alleged lack of impartiality or independence, stand as obstacles to a challenge being
mounted on the basis of disagreement or dissatisfaction with procedural decisions of the Tribunal.

2. The Calls for Deposits
72. The Respondents’ second main ground in support of the Challenge is that they have “justifiable doubts
as to the independence of the members of the Tribunal moneywise” because of the LCIA’s “insistence
on the payment of deposits, timely linked to the date at which procedural decisions were to be
rendered”. In this regard, the Respondents repeatedly state that they presume that the LCIA’s calls
for the payment of deposits were made pursuant to the Tribunal’s instructions (see, e.g., 12 November
Submission, para. 4.4.3).
73. Articles 24.1 and 24.3 of the Rules read as follows:
24.1 The LCIA Court may direct the parties, in such proportions and at such times as it thinks
appropriate, to make one or more payments to the LCIA on account of the Arbitration Costs. Such
payments deposited by the parties may be applied by the LCIA Court to pay any item of such
Arbitration Costs (including the LCIA’s own fees and expenses) in accordance with the LCIA Rules.
…
24.3 Save for exceptional circumstances, the Arbitral Tribunal should not proceed with the
arbitration without having ascertained from the Registrar that the LCIA is or will be in requisite funds
as regards outstanding and future Arbitration Costs.
74. As the provisions of Article 24.1 make clear, the decision to direct the Parties to make payments on
account of the Arbitration Costs is the LCIA Court’s decision, not the Tribunal’s. That said, under Article
24.3 of the Rules, the Tribunal should not proceed with the arbitration unless it has ascertained that
the LCIA “is or will be in requisite funds”. It is because of these provisions that it is appropriate for a
Tribunal, aware that directions for the payment of deposits have not been complied with, to remind
the Parties that funds must be deposited before it can proceed with the case.
75. The Respondents have failed to point to any facts likely to give rise to justifiable doubts as to the
Tribunal’s impartiality or independence “moneywise”. The decisions to make calls for deposits belong
to the LCIA Court, and these are made in an administrative capacity. Nothing suggests that any
Decision 13 - 22

influence was exerted in this case in order to seek to manipulate the financial decisions of the LCIA
Court to the detriment of the Respondents or, to cite the Respondents’ words, that the actions of
the Tribunal “might be dictated by something else than justice.” The Respondents’ invitation to draw
an adverse inference as to the Tribunal’s independence and impartiality from the calls for deposits
and the surrounding correspondence is, in my opinion, inapposite, and I have no hesitation in declining
it.
3. The Tribunal’s Reaction to the Late Receipt of the Claimant’s Deposit by the LCIA
76. The Respondents argue in their Supplementary Brief that the Tribunal had “no issue restricting
Respondents’ rights, and imposing Respondents sanctions without warning (the Tribunal’s 29.10.2018
Decision imposing new preconditions for the brief to fulfill within 4 days) but is incapable of doing
what it said it will do when it comes to sanction Claimant”(para. 64, at p. 12).
77. The first leg of this argument – which, in effect, reproaches the Tribunal for applying a double standard
– refers to the Respondents’ first ground for the Challenge, which I have rejected as being based on
an erroneous interpretation of the Tribunal’s 26 September Decision. The second leg of the argument
refers to the fact that the Claimant’s share of the deposit most recently directed by the LCIA Court
appears to have been received by the LCIA on 13 May 2019, which is after the deadline of 10 May
2019 set by the LCIA. Nonetheless, argue the Respondents, the Tribunal did not treat the Claimant’s
claims as withdrawn, as contemplated in earlier correspondence.
78. It is worth recalling the background to this issue. As noted earlier in this decision, upon the filing of
the Challenge, the Parties were reminded by the LCIA that neither of them had filed its share of the
deposit directed on 12 September 2018, and therefore that the LCIA did not have sufficient funds to
proceed with the Challenge. There followed an exchange of correspondence concerning the possible
application of Article 24.6 of the Rules, which reads as follows:

24.6 Failure by a claiming or cross-claiming party to make promptly and in full any required
payment on account of Arbitration Costs may be treated by the Arbitral Tribunal as a withdrawal from
the arbitration of the claim or cross-claim respectively, thereby removing such claim or cross-claim (as
the case may be) from the scope of the Arbitral Tribunal’s jurisdiction under the Arbitration
Agreement, subject to any terms decided by the Arbitral Tribunal as the reinstatement of the claim or

any claim or cross-claim made by another party.
79. The Respondents eventually took the position that the Tribunal should confirm that the Claimant’s

60 and 62 of the Supplementary Brief).
80. It is in that context that the Tribunal decided, on 16 May 2019, to stay the proceedings pending the

81. In relation to this sequence of events, the Respondents say that the decision to stay the proceedings
provide a further ground to challenge the Tribunal’s impartiality because it evidences the application

email of 16 May 2019).
82. I am not called upon to decide in the context of the present challenge whether the Tribunal was right
or wrong to suspend the proceedings. That decision falls within the Tribunal’s discretion under Articles
14.4 and 14.5 of the Rules and Section 33 of the Act. The contention I am presented with is that the
decision to stay the arbitration on 16 May 2019 gives rise to justifiable doubts as to the Tribunal’s
impartiality or independence.
Decision 13 - 24

83. I have no hesitation in rejecting this contention. It is recalled that prior to the Challenge being put in
abeyance pending payment of the funds requested by the LCIA pursuant to Article 24.1 of the Rules,
the Tribunal had been informed by the Respondents that they would no longer participate in the
proceedings in any way pending determination of the Challenge (see Respondents’ email of
1 November 2018, para. 2.3).
84. Later on the Respondents relied on the fact of the pending Challenge to seek to parse the options
provided for in Article 24.6, on the one hand insisting on the Tribunal confirming that the Claimant’s
claims are treated as withdrawn, but on the other hand denying it the possibility to consider whether,
in light of the payment made on 13 May 2019 and the explanation given by the Claimant for this
delayed payment, these claims should be reinstated.
85. In my opinion, a fair minded and informed observer, having considered the facts, would not see in the
Tribunal’s decision of 16 May 2019 a real possibility that the Tribunal was biased. It is not disputed
that the Tribunal had the discretion to stay the proceedings. In my opinion, its decision to do so in
light of the alternative presented to it by the Respondents in the context of the pending Challenge
does not raise a justifiable doubt as to the Tribunal’s impartiality.
4. The Tribunal’s email dated 1 November 2019
86. The Respondents have asserted that the Tribunal’s email dated 1 November 2019 provides further
ground for the Challenge.
87. This email was issued upon receipt by the Tribunal of the Respondents’ email of even date informing
the Tribunal and the LCIA Court of the Respondents’ decision to lodge the Challenge. By this
communication, the Tribunal reminded the Parties that “a Party’s indication that it intends to file a
challenge … does neither interrupt the procedural timetable, nor does it liberate the Parties from

complying with the directions of the Arbitral Tribunal.” The Respondents criticize the Tribunal for
failing to understand that the Respondents’ email of 1 November 2018 was not merely an indication
of an intent to challenge the Tribunal, but a clear indication that the independence and impartiality of
the Tribunal “is today … challenged”.
88. As seen already, the complete sentence from the Respondents’ email of 1 November 2018 is the
following: “The independence and impartiality of the three members of the Tribunal is today, and shall
be challenged in more detail within 14 days from the last communication from the Tribunal”. In light
of this language, I cannot see how the Tribunal can be reproached for describing this communication
as “a Party’s indication that it intends to file a challenge”.

arbitral proceedings, the Tribunal was merely expressing the position under the Rules, which do not
provide for the automatic suspension of the arbitration pending determination of a challenge. The

Conclusion
90. For all of the foregoing reasons, I conclude that none of the grounds for the Challenge raised by the
Respondents, taken individually or as a whole, gives rise to justifiable doubts as to the Tribunal’s
impartiality or independence
